A 29-year-old woman arrives at the emergency department with a one-day history of left forearm pain,
which started after several hours of typing at work. She denies any trauma or prior similar episodes.
Her medical history is unremarkable. On physical examination, there is medial deviation of the
olecranon and adduction of the wrist on the left side. Tenderness is noted around the proximal forearm,
but there is no swelling or erythema. The elbow's range of motion is normal. Which of the following
somatic dysfunctions is the most likely diagnosis? Answer Choices: (A) Abduction of the ulna (B)
Posterior translation of the ulna (C) Anterior translation of the ulna (D) Interosseous membrane
dysfunction (E) Supination of the radius (F) Ulnar head subluxation (G) Proximal radioulnar joint
dysfunction (H) Adduction of the ulna (I) Distal radioulnar joint dysfunction (J) Pronation of the radius
 A. Ulnar head subluxation
B. Posterior translation of the ulna
C. Anterior translation of the ulna
D. Interosseous membrane dysfunction
E. Abduction of the ulna
F. Supination of the radius
G. Adduction of the ulna
H. Distal radioulnar joint dysfunction
I. Pronation of the radius
J. Proximal radioulnar joint dysfunction
